reasons: The excerpt explicitly applies the brownie analogy to websites and directs: “remove any of those potential fears” so the next step is “extremely obvious and inviting.”
The candidate does not add a measurement threshold or claim a measured conversion outcome.
The excerpt explicitly praises “Try our 30-second claim checker” as having no perceived embarrassment and says it could not be a lower-commitment CTA.
The candidate presents this as language to use, without asserting that the exact phrase or duration is required in every setting.

The excerpt identifies “claim assessment” as somewhat technical and suggests explaining the benefits and outcomes, including whether there is a valid claim, likelihood of success, and possible compensation.
It also expressly calls out that the stronger CTA tells visitors what they will get.

The sequencing is supported as an example: injury details come first and name, email, and phone come at step two. However, the excerpt presents this as the design of a particular claim form, rather than establishing that every form must use exactly this sequence.

The exclusion improperly converts the problem being repaired into an exclusion. “Asking for personal information immediately” is the behavior the proposed action seeks to avoid, not a condition under which the action should be excluded.

For the stated condition—where results cannot be calculated live and need human intervention—the excerpt says the results page should explain that the claims team will contact the visitor to discuss the claim and provide results.

The excerpt expressly gives the intended consequence: stating this makes a follow-up call acceptable. The dependency on the preceding multi-step form is consistent with the described step-one, step-two, and step-three flow.

The excerpt observes that one particular claim-test page focuses on getting visitors to do the test rather than selling the solicitors’ firm. It does not establish a universal prohibition on selling a company on every CTA page.
The exclusion again turns the behavior being displaced—selling the firm on the CTA page—into an exclusion rather than stating it as the focus tradeoff or a page-specific recommendation.
The excerpt praises the specific kitchen-design wording as plain English, common sense, and fear-removing, but it does not establish that every CTA can or must remove “all possible fears.”

Its trigger is not supported by its cited quote: “It removes all of the possible fears” does not state that CTA wording can leave fears unresolved. The candidate should instead tie the action to identified visitor fears or objections.
The conditional home-address wording is supported for the free-home-survey example, and the excerpt explicitly praises not forcing an address when a survey is optional.

However, the exclusion improperly represents “Forcing the visitor to give their address” as an exclusion condition. That is the practice the action is intended to prevent, not an exception to the action.
The warning directly reflects the excerpt’s stated mistake: assuming people with questions will simply make contact.
The excerpt further supports the warning by stating that most people do initial scouting and will go elsewhere if they cannot determine whether the provider is in the right ballpark.

The excerpt expressly instructs the reader to use the boiler-repair scenario, identify questions and objections before contacting the first Google result, and says this puts the reader in the customer’s mindset.
The candidate retains the exercise as an exercise and does not invent a required number of responses.
The excerpt directly gives this as “the exercise for you”: identify the top three fears potential customers have about requesting the CTA.
The stated dependency is consistent with the excerpt’s sequence: after the customer-mindset exercise, “then” consider the top three fears.
The excerpt explicitly introduces the free-claim-assessment page as an example that “does a pretty good job.”
It subsequently says the wording addresses the main embarrassment objection for someone unsure whether they have a claim. The candidate appropriately avoids asserting measured performance.
The excerpt uses the kitchen-design CTA as the direct illustration of a highly clear invitation, comparing it to a sign that says “Please take one.”
It explicitly says this wording is plain English and removes possible fears, while the candidate makes no unsupported performance claim.
The source explicitly offers the Fat Witch brownie sign, together with a purchasable option after the visitor likes it, as a “better still” illustrative option.
The candidate correctly preserves it as an example and notes its non-immediate sequencing in the unknowns rather than recasting it as a required action.
The supplied excerpt ends mid-sentence at “It’s free, so how good is,” after beginning an Exposure Ninja-specific fear list.
The candidate accurately identifies this as unresolved due to the excerpt ending, without supplying missing content.
The excerpt says the wording is “really important” and “might be the most important wording on the website” because the visitor is about to decide whether to inquire.
The candidate preserves the source’s qualified “might be” framing and does not claim quantified conversion impact.

omissions.description: The excerpt gives a concrete checklist of information visitors may need before contacting a service provider: approximate price, response speed, reliability and who will attend, qualifications, compatibility with the visitor’s boiler type, and service area. The candidates include the exercise and general warning but do not retain these specific question categories.
omissions.quote: we need to know approximately how much it's going to cost. We need to know how quickly they can come because that's really important. We need to know are is the person good, reliable, who is actually coming out to do the boiler. Um, are they qualified? Do they work with my type of boiler? Do they service my area?

omissions.description: The excerpt provides a distinct rationale and follow-up wording for requesting contact details after problem details: explain that the details are needed to send the assessment to the visitor. The form-order candidate retains the sequence but not this explanatory copy or rationale.
omissions.quote: Great, thank you for filling out your injury details so that we can send your claim assessment to the right information, you know, to the right place. Tell us where to send it.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-sentence, so preceding framing and any earlier qualifications are unavailable.
The excerpt ends mid-sentence while introducing an Exposure Ninja-specific fear list; the rest of that list and any subsequent guidance are missing.
The material is a spoken/transcribed presentation with apparent transcription errors and repetitions, which can make exact intended wording uncertain.
The excerpt offers qualitative examples and opinions but provides no conversion data, testing method, or measured results for the cited pages.
Most implementation detail is illustrated through claim, kitchen-design, and boiler-repair examples; the excerpt does not establish universal applicability or required thresholds for all websites.
